sections.heading: MT940 Tag Structure Explained
paragraphs: Every MT940 file follows a strict tag hierarchy. The :20 tag carries a unique statement reference that identifies this particular export. The :25 tag names the account in IBAN or bank-local format, so the receiving system knows which account the transactions belong to.

Balance tags :60M and :62M bookend the transaction list with opening and closing figures. Each contains a credit-or-debit indicator, the date, a currency code and the amount. Accurate balances are mandatory because reconciliation software validates that the closing balance of one statement matches the opening balance of the next.

Individual transactions live in :61 lines with a compact date, amount and reference layout, while the :86 tag provides the free-text narrative. Matching each :61 with its :86 narrative keeps descriptions aligned with the correct line item, preventing the kind of orphaned entries that confuse auditors.

sections.heading: Handling Multi-Currency and Statement Periods
paragraphs: Companies operating across borders often maintain accounts in multiple currencies. Each currency requires its own statement block with the correct currency code in the balance tags. The converter generates separate statement sequences for each currency found in the workbook, keeping them properly delimited.

Statement period dates determine the :60M opening balance date and the :62M closing balance date. Getting these right matters for automated reconciliation, which compares closing and opening balances across consecutive statements to detect gaps or missing transactions.

Reference numbers in the :20 tag should follow your bank's convention, whether sequential, date-based or account-scoped. A consistent reference scheme makes it simpler to trace statements back to their source workbook when auditors ask questions months later.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
paragraphs: Date formatting is the most frequent source of rejection. MT940 requires YYMMDD without separators, but spreadsheets often store dates in locale-specific formats. The converter normalizes dates automatically, so a column of March 15 entries becomes 230315 in every :61 and balance line.

Missing or extra spaces in free-text :86 narratives cause parsers to misalign transaction details with their descriptions. The tool trims and pads narrative fields to the expected width, preventing the subtle spacing errors that surface only when the receiving bank processes the file.

Encoding mismatches between the spreadsheet and the MT940 output can corrupt non-ASCII characters in descriptions. The converter ensures UTF-8 consistency throughout, so Arabic, accented Latin and other scripts survive the round trip intact.
